title: Calamansi juice
intro: Freshly squeezed calamansi stretched with cold water and sweetened just enough to balance the sourness. It is bright, tart and very cold, the everyday juice for hot afternoons and for washing down fried food.

steps.text: Wash the calamansi and cut each one in half crosswise, just off center so most seeds stay in the smaller half.
Squeeze the halves over a small strainer set on a pitcher to catch the seeds. Squeeze firmly but do not twist the peel hard, or the juice turns bitter.
Stir the sugar into the warm water until it dissolves completely.
Add the syrup and cold water to the juice and stir. Taste and adjust with more sugar or water.
Fill glasses with ice and pour the juice over.

tips: The juice keeps for a day in a covered pitcher in the fridge. Add ice only to the glasses, never to the pitcher, so it does not get watery.

title: Hot calamansi juice
intro: Calamansi juice stirred into hot water with honey, a warm sweet-sour cup that many families make on rainy nights or before bed.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil, then take it off the heat and let it stand a minute or two so it is very hot but not boiling.
Halve the calamansi crosswise and squeeze them through a small strainer, dividing the juice between two mugs.
Add the honey to the mugs, pour in the hot water and stir until dissolved. Taste and add more honey or a squeeze more calamansi.

tips: Boiling water dulls the fresh calamansi flavor, so let it cool slightly first.

title: Salabat
intro: Fresh ginger simmered with brown sugar into a sweet, peppery hot drink. People drink it on cold mornings and rainy days, and at Christmas with puto bumbong or bibingka.

steps.text: Slice the ginger thinly, or smash it with the flat of a knife. There is no need to peel it if the skin is clean.
Put the ginger and water in a pot and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer until the water is pale gold and tastes strongly of ginger.
Stir in the sugar and simmer until it dissolves. Taste and add more sugar if you like it sweeter.
Strain into cups and serve hot.

tips: For a stronger, spicier salabat, grate the ginger instead of slicing it and strain through a fine sieve. Leftovers keep for 3 days in the fridge; reheat without boiling hard.

title: Tanglad tea
intro: Lemongrass stalks boiled into a light, lemony tea with a grassy sweetness, sometimes with a pandan leaf for extra fragrance. It is good hot after dinner or poured over ice in the afternoon.

steps.text: Trim off the dry tops and root ends of the lemongrass. Bruise the stalks along their length with the back of a knife, then fold or knot them so they fit the pot.
Put the lemongrass, pandan if using, and water in a pot and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer until the tea is pale yellow and fragrant.
Turn off the heat and let it steep, still covered.
Strain, sweeten to taste and serve hot, or cool it and pour over ice.

tips: Use the thick lower half of the stalks for the most flavor. The tea keeps for 3 days in the fridge.

title: Pandan iced tea
intro: Black tea brewed in pandan-infused water and sweetened, so it tastes like regular iced tea with a soft, vanilla-like pandan aroma. A pitcher of it goes well with a big merienda or a family lunch.

steps.text: Tie the pandan leaves into a loose knot so they are easy to fish out later.
Bring the water and pandan to a boil in a pot, then lower the heat and simmer until the water smells strongly of pandan and turns faintly green.
Turn off the heat, add the tea bags and steep. Do not steep longer, or the tea turns bitter.
Remove the tea bags and pandan, squeezing the leaves against the side of the pot. Stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Cool to room temperature, then pour into a pitcher and chill.
Serve in glasses filled with ice.

tips: Frozen pandan leaves work just as well as fresh. For a stronger pandan flavor, cut the leaves into short pieces before boiling and strain them out.

title: Sago't gulaman
intro: Chewy sago pearls and cubes of gulaman in cold water sweetened with brown sugar syrup (arnibal). It tastes of caramel and vanilla, and it is the drink sold from big jars by street vendors on hot days.

items.name: drops red or brown food coloring

steps.text: Make the gulaman first. Sprinkle the gulaman powder over the water in a pot and stir. Bring to a boil, stirring, and boil until fully dissolved. Stir in the food coloring if using.
Pour into a square pan and leave to set at room temperature, or in the fridge to speed it up.

Meanwhile, bring the 6 cups of water to a rolling boil and add the sago. Simmer, stirring now and then so it does not stick, until the pearls are mostly clear with only a small white dot in the center.
Turn off the heat, cover the pot and let the sago stand until the white centers disappear.
Drain the sago and rinse it under cold water to wash off the starch.
For the arnibal, simmer the brown sugar, water and pandan in a small pan until slightly syrupy. Take off the heat, remove the pandan and stir in the vanilla.
Cut the set gulaman into small cubes.
In a pitcher, stir together the arnibal, cold water, sago and gulaman. Taste and add more water or syrup.
Serve over ice with wide straws or a long spoon.

tips: Cooked sago turns hard and white in the fridge, so keep it in the syrup mixture and finish the pitcher within a day. Ready-cooked sago from the market saves the boiling step.

title: Buko juice
intro: Fresh young coconut water with strips of soft buko meat, served very cold. It is lightly sweet and nutty, and the strips give you something to chew between sips.

items.name: young coconuts (buko)
items.note: or 4 cups coconut water and 2 cups young coconut meat

steps.text: Lay a coconut on its side. With a heavy cleaver, shave the husk off the pointed top until you reach the hard shell.
Strike the exposed shell a few times in a circle with the heel of the cleaver to crack open a lid. Pour the water through a strainer into a pitcher. Repeat with the rest.
Split the coconuts open or widen the opening, then scrape out the soft meat with a sturdy spoon.
Cut the meat into long thin strips and add them to the coconut water.
Taste and stir in sugar only if needed. Serve over ice or chill well first.

tips: Most markets sell buko already opened, or sell the water and meat separately. Fresh coconut water tastes best the same day.

title: Buko shake
intro: Soft young coconut meat blended with its own water, condensed milk and ice into a thick, creamy, gently sweet shake.

steps.text: Blend the coconut meat and coconut water until smooth.
Add the condensed milk and ice and blend until thick and slushy.
Taste, blend in a little more condensed milk if you like, and pour into tall glasses.

tips: Soft, jelly-like buko blends smoothest. If yours is firm, blend it longer with the water before adding the ice.

title: Melon juice
intro: Long shreds of ripe cantaloupe floating in sweetened cold water, so you drink the juice and chew the fruit. It is light, fragrant and very refreshing on a hot day.

items.name: ripe cantaloupe
items.note: about 1.5 kg, fragrant at the stem end

steps.text: Halve the melon and scoop the seeds into a strainer set over a bowl. Press the seeds to collect their juice, then discard them.
Shred the flesh with a melon scraper, drawing it from the cut side down toward the rind to make long strands. Stop when you reach the pale green part near the rind.
Stir the sugar into the warm water until dissolved.
In a pitcher, combine the shredded melon, the collected juice, the syrup and cold water. Stir and taste for sweetness.
Chill so the melon flavors the water.
Serve over ice with spoons or wide straws.

tips: A melon scraper (kudkuran ng melon) is sold cheaply in markets; a coarse grater or a spoon also works, though the shreds are shorter.

title: Mango shake
intro: Ripe mangoes blended with ice, milk and a little condensed milk into a thick, sunny shake that tastes like pure mango. It is the most-ordered drink at any fruit shake stall.

steps.text: Slice the cheeks off the mangoes, score the flesh and scoop it into the blender. Scrape the flesh off the seed too.
Add the milk and condensed milk and blend until smooth.
Add the ice and blend until thick and frosty. Taste and adjust the sweetness.
Pour into glasses and serve right away.

tips: Freeze cubed ripe mango when it is in season and use it in place of some of the ice for a thicker shake.

title: Green mango shake
intro: Sour green mango blended with sugar and ice into a pale green shake that is tart, sweet and faintly salty. It wakes you right up on a hot afternoon.

steps.text: Peel the mangoes, slice the flesh off the seeds and chop it roughly.
Blend the mango with the sugar, water and salt until completely smooth.
Add the ice and blend until slushy. Taste: green mangoes vary a lot in sourness, so add more sugar as needed.
Pour into glasses and serve right away.

tips: Use firm, fully green mangoes with white or pale yellow flesh. Some stalls blend in a spoonful of condensed milk for a creamier version.

title: Avocado shake
intro: Ripe avocado blended with milk, condensed milk and ice into a thick, buttery, pale green shake. In the Philippines avocado is treated as a sweet fruit, and this is its most popular form.

steps.text: Halve the avocado, remove the seed and scoop the flesh into the blender.
Add the milk and condensed milk and blend until very smooth.
Add the ice and blend until thick. Taste and add more condensed milk if needed.
Pour into glasses and serve right away, before it starts to darken.

tips: The avocado should give slightly when pressed. An underripe one tastes grassy and will not blend smooth.

title: Ube shake
intro: Ube halaya blended with milk and ice into a thick purple shake that tastes sweet, milky and gently earthy, like a drinkable ube dessert.

steps.text: Blend the ube halaya and milk until smooth, with no lumps left.
Add the condensed milk and ice and blend until thick and frosty.
Taste and add more condensed milk if your halaya is not very sweet. Pour and serve.

tips: Without halaya, use 1 cup boiled and mashed ube with 3 tablespoons condensed milk and a little more milk.

title: Banana shake
intro: Ripe lakatan bananas blended with cold milk and ice into a thick, naturally sweet shake. It is quick enough for breakfast and filling enough for merienda.

steps.text: Peel the bananas and break them into the blender.
Add the milk and sugar and blend until smooth.
Add the ice and blend until thick and frothy. Pour and serve right away.

tips: Bananas with brown spots make the sweetest shake. Slice and freeze overripe ones and use them in place of the ice.

title: Strawberry shake
intro: Fresh strawberries blended with milk, condensed milk and ice into a pink, creamy, sweet-tart shake, the one you find wherever Benguet strawberries are sold.

steps.text: Rinse the strawberries, then pull or cut off the green tops.
Blend the strawberries with the milk and condensed milk until smooth.
Add the ice and blend until thick. Taste: tart berries may need another spoonful of condensed milk.
Pour into glasses and serve right away.

tips: Local strawberries are often quite tart; the condensed milk is what balances them. Frozen strawberries work in place of half the ice.

title: Fresh pineapple juice
intro: Ripe pineapple blended with water and strained into a sweet, tangy, frothy juice that tastes nothing like the canned kind.

steps.text: Cut off the crown and base of the pineapple, then slice off the skin from top to bottom. Remove the eyes with a small knife.
Quarter the pineapple lengthwise, cut out the hard core and chop the flesh into chunks.
Blend the chunks with 1 cup of the water until completely smooth. Work in batches if needed.
Pour through a fine sieve into a pitcher, pressing the pulp with a spoon to get all the juice out.
Stir in the rest of the water. Taste and add sugar only if the pineapple is not sweet enough.
Let the foam settle for a few minutes or skim it off, then serve over ice.

tips: A ripe pineapple smells sweet at the base and a leaf pulled from the center comes out easily. The juice is best on the day you make it.

title: Guyabano juice
intro: Ripe guyabano (soursop) blended with water and sugar and strained into a thick, milky-looking juice. It tastes like a mix of pineapple, banana and citrus, sweet with a sour finish.

steps.text: Peel the soft skin off the guyabano with your fingers and pull out the fibrous center core.
Pull the white flesh apart into segments and pop out every black seed. Discard the skin, core and seeds.
Put the flesh in a blender with 2 cups of the water and the sugar. Pulse briefly, just until the flesh breaks down, so any missed seeds are not crushed.
Pour through a sieve into a pitcher, pressing the pulp to get all the juice through.
Stir in the rest of the water and the calamansi juice if using. Taste and adjust the sugar.
Serve over ice.

tips: A guyabano is ripe when it gives like a ripe avocado and the skin darkens a little. You can freeze the seeded flesh in bags and make juice later.

title: Dalandan juice
intro: Juice squeezed from green-skinned dalandan, lightly sweetened and stretched with a little water. It is tangy and fragrant, sharper than orange juice and much less sour than calamansi.

steps.text: Roll each dalandan firmly on the counter to loosen the juice, then halve them crosswise.
Squeeze them on a citrus juicer and strain out the seeds and pulp you do not want.
Stir the sugar into the juice until it dissolves.
Add the cold water, taste, and adjust with more water or sugar. Serve over ice.

tips: Dalandan vary a lot in sweetness, so taste the juice before adding water and sugar. Skip the water entirely if the fruit is very sweet.

title: Tsokolate eh
intro: Thick, intensely chocolatey hot chocolate made from tablea (pure cacao tablets) and whisked until frothy. It coats a spoon and is served in small cups, often with suman or puto for dunking.

steps.text: Put the tablea and water in a small, heavy pot over medium-low heat. Stir until the tablea melts into the water.
Keep it at a gentle simmer, whisking often, until it has reduced and thickened noticeably. Do not let it boil hard or it scorches.
Add the milk, sugar and salt and simmer, whisking hard with a batirol (wooden whisk) or a wire whisk until thick and frothy.
Taste and add more sugar if you like. Pour into small cups and serve hot.

tips: Tablea is pure ground cacao, so a little grit at the bottom of the cup is normal. Whisk again right before pouring to bring back the froth.

title: Tsokolate
intro: The everyday thin hot chocolate made from tablea, water and sugar, with a splash of milk. It is rich and slightly bitter but light enough to drink by the mugful with pandesal at breakfast.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a pot, then lower the heat and add the tablea.
Simmer, stirring often, until the tablea has completely melted and the drink smells deeply of chocolate.
Stir in the sugar and milk and heat through without boiling.
Whisk hard or froth with a batirol until foamy on top. Taste for sweetness and serve hot.

tips: Tablea brands differ in strength. Start with 4 discs, and add one more next time if you want it richer.

title: Kapeng barako
intro: Strong brewed coffee from barako beans, heavy-bodied and bold with a slightly smoky, fruity bitterness. Many drink it black with a spoonful of muscovado, with pandesal or kakanin on the side.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a kettle or pot, then take it off the heat and let it stand for a moment.
Stir in the ground coffee, cover and let it steep.
Pour through a cloth coffee sock or a sieve lined with a paper filter into a warmed pot or carafe.
Serve hot in cups, with muscovado on the side for each person to sweeten.

tips: A French press works well for barako: steep 4 to 5 minutes, then press. Brewing past 6 minutes makes it harsh rather than strong.

title: Kape with condensed milk
intro: Hot coffee sweetened and whitened in one go with condensed milk, so it is creamy, caramel-sweet and still strong. It is the classic carinderia and kitchen-table cup.

items.name: hot brewed coffee
items.note: or 2 tsp instant coffee in 2 cups hot water

steps.text: Brew the coffee strong, or dissolve the instant coffee in freshly boiled water.
Spoon the condensed milk into two mugs.
Pour the hot coffee over and stir until the milk is fully dissolved. Taste and add more condensed milk if you like.

tips: Condensed milk sinks to the bottom, so stir well and give it a last stir before drinking.

title: Iced coffee
intro: Strong coffee sweetened with brown sugar, chilled and poured over ice with evaporated and condensed milk. It is creamy, sweet and bold, the Filipino home version of a coffee-shop iced latte.

steps.text: Brew the coffee about twice as strong as you would drink it hot, since the ice dilutes it.
Stir the brown sugar into the hot coffee until dissolved.
Cool the coffee to room temperature, then chill it in the fridge. This can be done a day ahead.
Stir the condensed milk into the evaporated milk.
Fill two tall glasses with ice, pour in the coffee and top with the milk mixture. Stir before drinking.

tips: Freeze leftover coffee in an ice tray and use the cubes in place of regular ice so the drink never gets watery.
